title: From Tires to Food The History of the Michelin Guide
paragraphs: Today, the Michelin Guide is one of the most respected restaurant guides in the world, and earning a Michelin star is a dream for many chefs. But the guide was created by a company that makes tires, not food.

In 1889, two brothers, André and Édouard Michelin, started a tire company in France. At that time, there were fewer than 3,000 cars in the country. The brothers wanted more people to drive, because more driving meant more tires would be needed.

So in 1900, they published the first Michelin Guide and gave it away for free. About 35,000 copies were printed. The small book was full of useful information for drivers, including maps, instructions for changing and repairing tires, and lists of hotels, restaurants and gas stations.

In 1920, the Michelin brothers started charging money for the guide. A few years later, in 1926, the guide began giving stars to restaurants that served excellent food. At first, there was only one star. In 1931, the system was expanded to the one, two and three stars that are still used today.

The stars have special meanings. One star means a very good restaurant in its category. Two stars mean excellent cooking that is worth a detour. Three stars mean exceptional food that is worth a special journey.

Restaurants are judged by anonymous inspectors. In 1936, the guide made its criteria public. They include the quality of the ingredients, the chef's skill and personal style, value for money and consistency. Decor and service are not part of the star rating.
Today, the Michelin Guide reviews restaurants in more than 30 countries. In 2025, France had 636 restaurants with stars, while Japan had 387.
